title: Assigning people to tasks identified in email: The EPA dataset for addressee tagging for detected task intent
abstract: Introduces the Enron People Assignment dataset, in which tasks described in authentic workplace emails are associated with the person or people responsible for carrying them out. The paper identifies both tasks and responsible people, defines evaluation methods, and evaluates a model against baselines. This is direct evidence for action-specific owner or assignee extraction.

title: Lin: Unsupervised Extraction of Tasks from Textual Communication
abstract: Studies extraction of specific tasks expressed through commitments and requests in emails and chat messages. Lin is an unsupervised approach based on dependency parsing and VerbNet and is evaluated across domains, including unseen domains. The work extracts task content rather than only predicting whether a message is actionable.

title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Team Collaborative Dialogue
abstract: Develops fine-grained dialogue analysis for authentic organizational Slack conversations in a software-development setting. The hierarchical annotation scheme includes collaborative acts such as proposals, requests, assignments, and rejections, and the work evaluates a transformer-plus-CRF architecture using long-range context. It is direct enterprise-chat evidence for distinguishing several action and decision-related communicative acts, although it is not a complete structured action benchmark.

title: Domain Adaptation for Commitment Detection in Email
abstract: Studies detection of commitments to future actions in email and demonstrates substantial domain bias when models are transferred between email corpora. It evaluates feature-level, sample-level, and representation-based domain adaptation for commitment detection. The target is genuine future-action commitment rather than generic modality or capability.

title: Monitoring Commitments in People-Driven Service Engagements
abstract: Models and detects commitments in real-world email and chat service engagements, including commitment creation as well as later delegation, completion, and cancellation. Evaluation uses the Enron email corpus and an HP IT-support chat dataset. The commitment representation captures who is responsible to whom for achieving what, with circumstances as part of the underlying semantics, although the paper does not establish separate field-level accuracy for all such arguments.
venue: 2013 IEEE International Conference on Services Computing

title: A Corpus-Based Classification of Commitments in Business English
abstract: Presents a corpus-based study of commitments in authentic Business English emails using a speech-act-annotated corpus. It distinguishes action, informational, and interactional commitments and analyzes their lexical and phraseological realizations. This provides direct workplace-email evidence about commitment categories, though not a joint structured argument extractor.
venue: Yearbook of Corpus Linguistics and Pragmatics 2013

title: Routine politeness in American and British English requests: use and non-use of please
abstract: Uses two comparable workplace email corpora that were pragmatically annotated so request speech acts can be retrieved independently of their surface formulation. The study analyzes 675 requests from each corpus and examines linguistic properties including mood and modal-verb use. It supplies direct empirical request annotation in workplace email, but does not evaluate structured owner or deadline extraction.

title: Making requests at work: An examination of phrase frames in workplace email communication
abstract: Analyzes 1,148 authentic request emails from the Avocado Research Email Collection. The study examines five-word phrase frames across rhetorical moves in workplace request emails and provides empirical evidence about how requests are linguistically realized. It is relevant to request identification and annotation but does not itself provide structured action arguments.

title: Context-Aware Intent Identification in Email Conversations
abstract: Studies sentence-level intent identification in workplace email using a large publicly available enterprise email dataset and models message and conversational context. The intent taxonomy includes action-relevant categories rather than only broad topical classes, with requests and future-action intents among the studied phenomena. It remains intent classification rather than full argument extraction.

title: Learning with Weak Supervision for Email Intent Detection
abstract: Uses user interaction logs as weak supervision for detecting actionable intents in email, combined with clean annotated data and self-paced learning. Experiments cover multiple email intent-detection tasks, including request- and action-related intents. The work provides direct empirical email evidence for communicative intent detection but not structured owner, deadline, or condition arguments.

title: Coding Dialogs with the DAMSL Annotation Scheme
abstract: Describes the DAMSL dialogue-act annotation scheme and reports its application to dialogue coding. Forward-looking functions include influencing the addressee's future action and committing the speaker to future action, while backward-looking functions include agreement and relations to antecedent discourse. This is foundational transfer evidence for distinguishing directives, commitments, and agreement rather than workplace-email evidence.
venue: AAAI Fall Symposium on Communicative Action in Humans and Machines

title: Dialogue Act Modeling for Automatic Tagging and Recognition of Conversational Speech
abstract: Develops statistical dialogue-act tagging on 1,155 hand-labeled Switchboard telephone conversations, with labels including agreement and disagreement alongside questions and statements. The work combines lexical, prosodic, and dialogue-sequence evidence. It is transfer evidence for contextual dialogue-act modeling, not direct workplace communication evidence.

title: The Berkeley FrameNet Project
abstract: Introduces FrameNet's corpus-based representation of semantic frames and frame elements, with annotated attestations linking semantic roles to their syntactic realizations. The approach provides transferable machinery for representing action participants, recipients, times, and other arguments. It does not by itself establish task ownership or workplace obligation semantics.

title: Automatic Labeling of Semantic Roles
abstract: Develops automatic semantic-role labeling using FrameNet-style predicate-argument structures. The work is foundational transfer evidence for extracting predicate-specific participants and adjuncts from text. Semantic agents should not be equated with assigned workplace owners, but the argument-extraction methods are relevant to structured action representations.

title: The Proposition Bank: An Annotated Corpus of Semantic Roles
abstract: Introduces PropBank, which adds predicate-argument semantic-role annotations to the Penn Treebank and supports automatic role labeling. Its explicit predicate-specific argument spans are useful transfer evidence for structured action extraction and evidence provenance. The roles describe event semantics rather than communicative responsibility.

title: Multi-Predicate Semantic Role Labeling
abstract: Addresses semantic-role labeling when multiple predicates occur in the same sentence rather than treating predicates independently. The method models interactions among predicates and their arguments. This is transfer evidence for binding arguments to the correct action when several actions coexist, not direct workplace-owner extraction.

title: Semantic Role Labeling of Implicit Arguments for Nominal Predicates
abstract: Introduces a manually annotated corpus of implicit arguments for ten NomBank predicates and trains a discriminative model to recover arguments absent from a predicate's local context. The work demonstrates discourse-sensitive recovery of omitted participants. It is transfer evidence for implicit-owner research, but its semantic arguments are not workplace assignees.

title: Inducing Implicit Arguments from Comparable Texts: A Framework and Its Applications
abstract: Develops a framework for inducing and resolving implicit predicate arguments by exploiting comparable texts. The approach addresses participants that are not overtly realized in the local predicate context. It is transfer evidence for recovering implicit actors or owners from broader discourse, while not directly modeling workplace responsibility.

title: Refining Implicit Argument Annotation for UCCA
abstract: Proposes a fine-grained typology for implicit arguments and annotates a subset of the UCCA English Web Treebank with categories including deictic, generic, genre-based, type-identifiable, non-specific, and iterated-set arguments. The resource is useful transfer evidence for distinguishing different sources of omitted participants. It does not directly annotate workplace task ownership.
venue: Second International Workshop on Designing Meaning Representations

title: Trigger is Not Sufficient: Exploiting Frame-aware Knowledge for Implicit Event Argument Extraction
abstract: Studies implicit event-argument extraction and proposes a frame-aware method that reasons from other arguments in the event frame rather than relying only on the event trigger. Curriculum knowledge distillation allows the final model to operate without oracle arguments. This is transfer evidence for context-dependent recovery of omitted action participants.

title: Explicit, Implicit, and Scattered: Revisiting Event Extraction to Capture Complex Arguments
abstract: Introduces DiscourseEE, an event-extraction dataset with explicit, implicit, and scattered event arguments, showing that important arguments may require contextual inference or evidence distributed across a document. The dataset contains 7,464 argument annotations from online health discourse. It is transfer evidence for implicit and non-contiguous action arguments rather than direct workplace communication evidence.

title: A Structured Learning Approach to Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Models temporal relations between events using structured learning so that dependencies among multiple temporal relations are considered jointly. The method addresses missing relations and improves over approaches that make independent pairwise decisions. It is transfer evidence for action-to-time reasoning, not direct deadline extraction from workplace messages.

title: A Multi-Axis Annotation Scheme for Event Temporal Relations
abstract: Proposes a multi-axis annotation scheme for temporal relations among events and refines the task by focusing temporal comparison on event start points. The work reports an expert annotation study and is aimed at improving consistency of event-time structure. It is transfer evidence for explicit temporal linking rather than a workplace deadline benchmark.

title: Joint Reasoning for Temporal and Causal Relations
abstract: Jointly extracts temporal and causal relations using constrained inference, exploiting logical interactions between the two relation types. The formulation enforces global consistency rather than making isolated relation predictions. It is transfer evidence for linking temporal expressions or events to particular actions in structured extraction.

title: Fine-Grained Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Introduces a fine-grained semantic framework that maps event pairs to real-valued temporal relations and durations and uses it to annotate the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank. Models jointly predict temporal relations and event durations. This is transfer evidence for richer action-time binding beyond standalone TIMEX detection.

title: Deep Structured Neural Network for Event Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Combines a neural pairwise temporal-relation scorer with structured inference enforcing constraints such as temporal transitivity. It is evaluated on multiple event temporal-relation datasets. The work is useful transfer evidence for maintaining consistent action-time relations but does not distinguish task deadlines in workplace communication.

title: A Modality Lexicon and its use in Automatic Tagging
abstract: Defines a modality annotation scheme centered on three linked components: modality trigger, target, and holder, and develops a modality lexicon plus automatic taggers. The explicit trigger-to-target representation is relevant to attaching modal meaning to the correct action rather than assigning only a sentence-level modality label. It is transfer evidence and does not specifically establish workplace commitment extraction.

title: The BioScope corpus: biomedical texts annotated for uncertainty, negation and their scopes
abstract: Introduces a corpus with token-level annotations for negation and uncertainty cues and sentence-level annotations of their linguistic scopes. Independent annotators and adjudication were used to construct the resource. This is transfer evidence for linking negation or uncertainty cues to the textual material they govern, not direct evidence for negated workplace obligations.

title: FactBank: a corpus annotated with event factuality
abstract: Presents FactBank, a corpus layered over TimeBank with annotations describing the factuality of events as conveyed by discourse. The representation captures distinctions between actual, non-occurring, and uncertain events arising from interacting linguistic markers. It is transfer evidence for event-level modality and negation attachment, not workplace deontic obligation extraction.

title: A general framework for information extraction using dynamic span graphs
abstract: Introduces an information-extraction framework that represents candidate textual spans as nodes and dynamically propagates information through predicted relation and coreference links. The approach jointly supports multiple span-oriented IE tasks and handles nested spans. It is transfer evidence for evidence-span-preserving structured extraction and cross-span argument relations.

title: Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction with Contextualized Span Representations
abstract: Presents DyGIE++, a unified span-based framework for entity, relation, and event extraction that scores text spans while incorporating local and cross-sentence context. Dynamic span graphs and coreference links support longer-range argument interactions. It is transfer evidence for retaining textual evidence spans while building structured records.

title: Span-Based Joint Entity and Relation Extraction with Transformer Pre-Training
abstract: Introduces SpERT, which searches over textual spans to jointly recognize entities and classify relations between them using transformer representations. Its explicit span-and-relation formulation provides transferable machinery for source-span provenance and argument binding. The evaluated tasks are generic entity and relation extraction rather than workplace actions.

title: Event Extraction by Answering (Almost) Natural Questions
abstract: Reformulates event argument extraction as extractive question answering, directly selecting argument spans for roles without requiring a separate entity-recognition stage. The method also evaluates extraction of roles unseen during training. It is transfer evidence for role-specific evidence spans and structured argument extraction rather than direct workplace action semantics.

title: Prompt for Extraction? PAIE: Prompting Argument Interaction for Event Argument Extraction
abstract: Presents an extractive event-argument model with role-specific span selectors and multi-role prompts so interactions among arguments are modeled jointly. Bipartite matching supports optimal span assignment, and the method can extract multiple arguments sharing the same role at sentence and document level. It is strong transfer evidence for action-specific span binding when several arguments coexist, but it is not a workplace obligation benchmark.
